title: Queues
summary: A **queue** is a linear structure where the oldest waiting item is handled first.
refresher: A **queue** follows **FIFO**: first in, first out. Use **enqueue** to add to the back, **dequeue** to remove from the front, and **peek** to read the front without removing it.
refresher_code:
enqueue A, enqueue B, enqueue C
dequeue -> A

advanced-queue-fifo.title: FIFO means oldest first
advanced-queue-fifo.body: A **queue** removes the item that has been waiting the longest.
advanced-queue-fifo.example: enqueue A, enqueue B, enqueue C, dequeue -> A
advanced-queue-fifo.notice: Add at the back. Remove from the front.
advanced-queue-fifo.mistake: Removing C first turns the behavior into a **stack**.

advanced-queue-bfs.title: Queues fit level-by-level work
advanced-queue-bfs.body: BFS uses a **queue** so **nodes** discovered first are processed first.
advanced-queue-bfs.example: visit start, enqueue neighbors, remove oldest neighbor next
advanced-queue-bfs.mistake: A **stack** would dive down one path instead of moving level by level.

advanced-queue-trace.title: Trace the front
advanced-queue-trace.body: When tracing a **queue**, track the front and back separately.
advanced-queue-trace.mistake: If you remove from the same end you added to, it is not **FIFO**.

advanced-queue-mistake.title: Back removal breaks FIFO
advanced-queue-mistake.body: A **queue** adds at the back and removes from the front.
advanced-queue-mistake.example: add A, add B, remove should return A
advanced-queue-mistake.mistake: Adding and removing at the back behaves like a **stack**.

sections.title: What is a queue?
sections.summary: A **queue** is **FIFO**: first in, first out.

blocks.body: A **queue** is a linear **data structure**. It stores items in arrival order. The first item added waits at the front and is the first item removed.

blocks.title: Watch FIFO in action
blocks.caption: Step through enqueue and dequeue so front and back are clear.

state.note: A queue removes the oldest item first.

variables_after.name: state
variables_after.value: A queue removes the oldest item first.

steps.title: Dequeue
steps.body: A **leaves** first because A waited the longest.
steps.decision: A **leaves** first because A waited the longest.
steps.why: A **leaves** first because A waited the longest.

blocks.body: That rule is called **FIFO**, which stands for first in, first out. Think about a line at a help desk. The person who arrived first should be helped first.

blocks.title: Queue vocabulary
items: `front` is where the next item **leaves**.
`back` or `rear` is where a new item joins.
`enqueue` means add an item to the back.
`dequeue` means remove and **return** the front item.
`peek` or `front` means look at the front item without removing it.
`is_empty` checks whether there is anything to remove.

blocks.caption: Trace the **FIFO** rule by hand before writing code.

python.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("A")
queue.append("B")
queue.append("C")
print(queue.popleft())
print(queue.popleft())

blocks.prompt: A **queue** receives A, then B, then C. What is removed first?
blocks.why: A arrived first, so A is at the front.

sections.title: The Queue ADT
sections.summary: A **queue** has two ends: add at the back, remove from the front.

blocks.body: A **queue** **ADT** describes the operations a queue must support. You can build the inside with an **array**, a **linked list**, or a library structure. The outside behavior should still be **FIFO**.

blocks.title: Queue operations
items: `enqueue(item)`: add item to the back.
`dequeue()`: remove and **return** the front item.
`peek()`: **return** the front item without removing it.
`is_empty()`: **return** true if the **queue** has no items.
`size()`: **return** how many items are stored.

blocks.caption: A **queue** uses opposite ends.
blocks.wrong: add A, add B, remove B
blocks.right: add A, add B, remove A
blocks.body: If the same end handles add and remove, the newest item **leaves** first. That is not **FIFO**.

blocks.title: Do not confuse dequeue and deque
blocks.body: `dequeue` is the action of removing from the front. `deque`, pronounced deck, is a double-ended **queue** **data type**.

blocks.prompt: Which operation adds an item to the back of a **queue**?
blocks.why: Enqueue is the **queue** word for adding at the back.

sections.title: Implement a queue
sections.summary: A beginner **queue** can use a **list**, but some structures are better for front removal.

blocks.body: A simple queue can store items in a **list**: **append** to the back and remove from the front. That teaches the idea well. For larger inputs, many languages offer a deque or queue **class** so front removal stays fast.

blocks.caption: A small **queue** **class** shows the basic operations.

blocks.title: Read the Python class line by line
items: `__init__` creates an empty **list**.
`enqueue` uses `append` because new items join at the back.
`dequeue` uses `pop(0)` because the front item is at **index** 0.
`peek` returns `items[0]` without removing it.
`size` uses `len` to count the stored items.

blocks.title: Performance note
blocks.body: Python `pop(0)` is simple but shifts the remaining items. `collections.deque` is better when you need many fast **queue** operations.

sections.title: Trace queue state
sections.summary: Draw both ends before you change the queue.

blocks.body: **Queue** bugs usually come from mixing up the **front** and the **back**. Mark both ends while tracing so you know where the next item leaves and where a new item joins.

blocks.title: Trace
items: start: []
enqueue 4 -> front [4] back
enqueue 9 -> front [4, 9] back
dequeue -> removes 4, **queue** becomes [9]
enqueue 2 -> front [9, 2] back

blocks.prompt: After enqueue 4, enqueue 9, dequeue, enqueue 2, what is at the front?
blocks.why: The dequeue removes 4. The oldest remaining item is 9.

sections.title: Deque, circular queue, and priority queue
sections.summary: **Queue** ideas grow into several useful variations.

blocks.body: A basic **queue** is **FIFO**. A **deque** lets you add or remove from both ends. A **circular queue** uses a fixed-size **array** and wraps around instead of shifting items. A **priority queue** removes the highest-priority item first instead of the oldest item.

blocks.title: Queue family
items: **Queue**: oldest item leaves first.
Deque: both ends are open for add and remove.
Circular **queue**: fixed space, front and back wrap around.
**Priority queue**: priority decides who leaves first.
**Heap**: a common way to implement a **priority queue** efficiently.

blocks.title: Why heaps belong later
blocks.body: A heap is not just another queue **method**. It needs its own lesson because students must learn the tree-like shape, parent/child **indexes**, and how **values** move up or down.

sections.title: Where queues show up
sections.summary: **Queues** are used when work should be handled in arrival order.

blocks.title: Common queue uses
items: Task scheduling: first waiting task gets handled first.
**Print** jobs: documents wait their turn.
Breadth-first search: **nodes** discovered first are **visited** first.
Streams and buffers: incoming work waits safely instead of being dropped immediately.
Round-robin scheduling: each task gets a turn, then goes to the back if more work remains.

blocks.caption: BFS uses a **queue** to visit level by level.

blocks.title: BFS needs queue order
blocks.body: If you use a **stack** instead, the code may still visit **nodes**, but it will not be breadth-first.

blocks.title: Use a queue for BFS order
blocks.caption: Watch BFS process the oldest waiting **node** before newer neighbors.

steps.title: Start at A
steps.body: A is discovered first, so A goes into the **queue**.
steps.what_changed: The **queue** stores work in discovery order.
steps.decision: The **queue** stores work in discovery order.
steps.why: A is discovered first, so A goes into the **queue**.

steps.title: Remove A
steps.body: A **leaves** the front. Its neighbors B and C are discovered next.
steps.what_changed: B and C join the back, behind any older work.
steps.decision: B and C join the back, behind any older work.
steps.why: A **leaves** the front. Its neighbors B and C are discovered next.

steps.title: Remove B
steps.body: B was waiting longer than C, so B is processed next.
steps.what_changed: This is what makes BFS move level by level.
steps.decision: This is what makes BFS move level by level.
steps.why: B was waiting longer than C, so B is processed next.
